articles.title: Rare breeding bat found roosting near reservoir
articles.summary: The Nathusius' pipistrelle is believed to be the first confirmed discovery of its kind in the area.
articles.content:
A rare species of breeding bat has been found roosting in woodland near a reservoir.

The Nathusius' pipistrelle has been confirmed at a Yorkshire Water site near Sheffield, the first time it had been recorded in South Yorkshire.

Environmental DNA (eDNA) collected from a bat box in March indicated the animal's presence, and in April one was physically spotted at another nearby bat box.

Lead ecologist at Yorkshire Water, Sean Davey, said: "The bat boxes on the Sheffield site were installed only nine months prior - so it's encouraging to see them being quickly adopted by multiple bat species."

The bat boxes were funded by Yorkshire Water's species conservation programme and installed in 2025. They were designed to mimic the natural features bats used for roosting, enhancing their habitats and helping bat populations to thrive on its sites.

Davey said DNA swabs were trialled by ecologists from Yorkshire Water and the South Yorkshire Bat Group.

He said: "Bat boxes and other known roost sites were swabbed to collect eDNA samples, revealing the presence of the rare migrant bat."
articles.reasoning: The article reports the confirmed discovery of a rare breeding bat species in a new area, indicating successful conservation efforts through habitat enhancement. This has broad environmental significance for biodiversity and species protection, with detailed context on the conservation methods and ecological monitoring.

articles.title: The Atlantic Ocean can handle more warming than expected — with one big catch
articles.summary: Scientists have found that the AMOC may be far more vulnerable to rapid warming than to temperature alone. When warming happens slowly, the ocean can adapt, but at faster rates similar to today’s, the massive Atlantic circulation could reach a tipping point at much lower temperatures.
articles.content:
For years, climate scientists have warned that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) could eventually shut down if global temperatures rise too far. New findings from researchers at Utrecht University suggest that temperature alone does not determine the fate of this major ocean circulation system. The speed at which the planet warms also appears to play a critical role in whether the AMOC remains stable. The study was published in the scientific journal Nature Climate Change.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC, is a vast network of ocean currents that carries warm water northward from the tropics. By moving heat around the planet, it strongly influences the global climate and helps maintain the relatively mild conditions found in Western Europe.

Scientists have long viewed this Atlantic 'heat engine' as a system that could cross a tipping point. If that happened, the AMOC could transition from its current strong circulation to a much weaker state within decades. Possible triggers include growing amounts of meltwater entering the ocean from polar regions as well as global warming itself.

Rethinking the AMOC Temperature Threshold

Researchers previously estimated that the AMOC could reach a tipping point and collapse at around +4°C of global warming. Scientists at the Institute for Marine and Atmospheric research Utrecht now say that this temperature threshold does not tell the whole story.

"Our results show there is not necessarily a fixed temperature beyond which the AMOC inevitably collapses," says lead author René van Westen. "The stability of the circulation depends on how fast the climate is changing."

The findings indicate that two worlds reaching the same eventual temperature could experience very different outcomes for the AMOC depending on how quickly the warming occurred.

Slow Warming Versus Fast Warming

To test the importance of warming speed, Van Westen and his colleagues ran two versions of a climate model. In both simulations, atmospheric CO 2 increased gradually, but the rate of that increase differed substantially.

In one simulation, CO2 concentrations increased slowly (0.5 ppm per year). In the second, they climbed much more rapidly (2.5 ppm per year), which is comparable to today's rate.

The contrast produced dramatically different results. When warming occurred slowly, the AMOC remained stable well beyond +4°C and did not collapse even after warming reached +5°C. Under the faster warming scenario, however, the AMOC collapsed at around +2°C.

"We deliberately looked at a scenario that is much slower than what we're experiencing today," explains co-author Reyk Börner. "That allowed us to isolate the effect of the warming rate alone, independent of how warm it eventually gets."

Why the Ocean Needs Time to Adapt

The researchers say the difference comes down to the ocean's ability to respond to changing conditions.

"Under slow warming, the entire ocean, from the surface down to its deepest layers, has time to gradually reorganize and adapt to the changing conditions," says co-author Henk Dijkstra, professor of Dynamical Oceanography. "Under faster warming, the ocean simply can't keep up."

Slow climate change gives the ocean more time to adjust throughout its full depth. When temperatures rise more rapidly, those adjustments cannot happen quickly enough, leaving the circulation more vulnerable to instability.

A Critical Rate of Global Warming

According to the researchers, the critical warming rate is around 0.3°C per decade. The world is already approaching that pace.

Van Westen compares the situation to driving a car: "If you're driving toward a wall, it makes sense to steer around it. To do that, you need to brake, otherwise you fly off the road. When it comes to global warming, the world is still pressing extra hard on the accelerator right now."

The analogy highlights an important distinction. Avoiding dangerous climate changes may depend not only on limiting how warm the planet eventually becomes, but also on slowing how quickly it gets there.

Previous Research on AMOC Stability

The same research group has investigated AMOC stability from several different perspectives in recent years.

In 2024, the researchers found that increasing amounts of meltwater entering the North Atlantic make the AMOC less stable. Scientists had suspected this mechanism for years, but the research was the first to demonstrate it using a modern, complex climate model.

Those results showed that a critical meltwater threshold exists, beyond which the AMOC becomes unstable. However, the threshold was unrealistically high. This suggests that the present-day AMOC is unlikely to become unstable through this contribution alone. That study did not include the effects of global warming or the pace at which warming occurs.

A later study explored several global warming scenarios. It concluded that the AMOC could reach a tipping point around 2060 under both an intermediate- and high-emission scenario. In those simulations, the tipping point occurred at approximately 2.5°C of global warming.

The latest research helps explain why studies can produce different estimates for when the AMOC might reach a tipping point, as well as why temperature thresholds vary across climate models and emissions scenarios.

The AMOC does appear to have a critical threshold for meltwater, but the researchers find no universal temperature threshold for its collapse. Instead, its stability depends partly on how quickly the planet warms. Faster warming leaves the AMOC more vulnerable, while slower warming gives the ocean more time to adjust and allows the circulation to remain stable under substantially higher levels of global warming.

What the Findings Mean for Climate Policy

The findings suggest that slowing the pace of warming could reduce the near-term risk of an AMOC collapse by giving the Atlantic Ocean more time to adapt.

That could have important implications for climate policy. Much of current climate policy, including the Paris Agreement, focuses on limiting the eventual peak in global temperature.

Some strategies involve so-called overshoot pathways. Under these approaches, global temperatures would temporarily rise beyond a target limit, with the expectation that future technologies could later reduce temperatures again.

The new findings suggest that the path taken toward a given temperature may matter alongside the temperature itself. The faster global warming occurs, the less time the Atlantic Ocean has to adjust, potentially increasing the vulnerability of one of the planet's most important circulation systems.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific finding that the Atlantic Ocean's major circulation system (AMOC) is more resilient to warming if the rate of warming is slower, highlighting the importance of slowing climate change to prevent collapse. This insight has broad implications for global climate policy and offers a hopeful perspective that managing the pace of warming can reduce risks to a critical climate system.
articles.personality_title: Slower warming helps Atlantic Ocean’s circulation stay strong longer
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a huge system of ocean currents that moves warm water from the tropics toward northern regions. This system plays a key role in keeping Western Europe’s climate mild and affects weather around the world. Scientists have worried that rising global temperatures could cause the AMOC to weaken or even collapse, which might change climates dramatically.

**What happened** – Researchers at Utrecht University studied how the speed of global warming affects the AMOC. They ran climate models with two different rates of carbon dioxide increase: one slow and one fast, like today’s rate. They found that if warming happens slowly, the AMOC can stay stable even at higher temperatures. But if warming happens quickly, the AMOC could collapse at much lower temperatures, around 2°C of warming.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that it’s not just how hot the Earth gets, but also how fast it warms that matters for the ocean’s health. The ocean needs time to adjust to changes, and fast warming doesn’t give it that chance. This explains why previous studies gave different predictions about when the AMOC might weaken. It also means slowing down the rate of warming could help protect this important ocean system.

**What’s next step** – Scientists and policymakers can use this new information to focus on slowing the pace of global warming, not just limiting the final temperature increase. This could influence climate agreements and strategies to avoid crossing dangerous tipping points in the ocean and climate.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Atlantic Ocean’s major circulation is more likely to stay stable if global warming happens slowly, highlighting the importance of reducing how quickly Earth’s temperature rises.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un réchauffement plus lent aide la circulation océanique atlantique à rester stable plus longtemps
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La circulation méridionale de retournement de l’Atlantique (AMOC) est un vaste système de courants marins qui transporte l’eau chaude des tropiques vers le nord. Ce système joue un rôle clé pour maintenir un climat doux en Europe de l’Ouest et influence le climat mondial. Les scientifiques craignent que la montée des températures mondiales ne fragilise ou n’arrête ce courant, ce qui pourrait bouleverser le climat.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université d’Utrecht ont étudié l’effet de la vitesse du réchauffement climatique sur l’AMOC. Ils ont simulé deux scénarios avec des taux d’augmentation différents du dioxyde de carbone : un lent et un rapide, proche du taux actuel. Ils ont découvert qu’un réchauffement lent permet à l’AMOC de rester stable même à des températures plus élevées. En revanche, un réchauffement rapide peut entraîner son effondrement dès environ +2°C.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que ce n’est pas seulement la température finale qui compte, mais aussi la vitesse à laquelle elle monte pour la santé de l’océan. L’océan a besoin de temps pour s’adapter aux changements, et un réchauffement rapide l’en empêche. Cela explique pourquoi les études précédentes donnaient des prédictions différentes sur la stabilité de l’AMOC. Cela signifie aussi qu’un ralentissement du réchauffement pourrait protéger ce système océanique vital.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques et décideurs peuvent utiliser ces nouvelles données pour insister sur la nécessité de ralentir le rythme du réchauffement, pas seulement de limiter la température finale. Ceci pourrait influencer les accords climatiques et les stratégies pour éviter des points de basculement dangereux.

**Phrase clé** – La circulation océanique majeure de l’Atlantique est plus stable si le réchauffement climatique est lent, soulignant l’importance de réduire la vitesse à laquelle la température de la Terre augmente.
articles.personality_title_es: Un calentamiento más lento ayuda a que la circulación del Atlántico se mantenga fuerte por más tiempo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La Circulación Meridional de Vuelco del Atlántico (AMOC) es un gran sistema de corrientes oceánicas que lleva agua caliente desde los trópicos hacia el norte. Este sistema es importante para mantener un clima suave en Europa Occidental y afecta el clima mundial. Los científicos han advertido que el aumento de la temperatura global podría debilitar o detener esta circulación, lo que cambiaría el clima.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Utrecht estudiaron cómo la velocidad del calentamiento global afecta al AMOC. Ejecutaron modelos climáticos con dos tasas diferentes de aumento de dióxido de carbono: una lenta y otra rápida, similar a la actual. Descubrieron que si el calentamiento es lento, el AMOC puede mantenerse estable incluso a temperaturas más altas. Pero si el calentamiento es rápido, el AMOC podría colapsar a temperaturas más bajas, cerca de 2°C.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo muestra que no solo importa qué tan caliente se pone la Tierra, sino también qué tan rápido se calienta para la salud del océano. El océano necesita tiempo para adaptarse a los cambios, y el calentamiento rápido no le da esa oportunidad. Esto explica por qué estudios anteriores daban diferentes predicciones sobre cuándo podría debilitarse el AMOC. También significa que desacelerar el calentamiento podría ayudar a proteger este sistema oceánico importante.

**Próximo paso** – Científicos y responsables de políticas pueden usar esta información para enfocarse en reducir la velocidad del calentamiento global, no solo en limitar la temperatura final. Esto podría influir en acuerdos climáticos y estrategias para evitar puntos de quiebre peligrosos en el océano y el clima.

**Frase clave** – La gran circulación del Atlántico es más estable si el calentamiento global ocurre lentamente, mostrando la importancia de reducir la rapidez con que aumenta la temperatura de la Tierra.

articles.title: Volunteer Develops Machine-Learning Tool to Identify Rare Clouds
articles.summary: Certain kinds of clouds are misbehaving – appearing more often and lower in the sky than they used to. To help identify the factors influencing these changes, scientists have asked people around the world with cameras to submit fresh images of these clouds as a part of the NASA-supported Space Cloud Watch project.
articles.content:
Certain kinds of clouds are misbehaving – appearing more often and lower in the sky than they used to. To help identify the factors influencing these changes (e.g. shifts in Earth’s long-term weather patterns), scientists have asked people around the world with cameras to submit fresh images of these clouds as a part of the NASA-supported Space Cloud Watch project. Now, one volunteer has developed a new tool to help other Space Cloud Watch volunteers work more efficiently.

The misbehaving clouds are “noctilucent” or “night-shining” clouds (NLCs). These clouds scatter light from the Sun long after sunset and long before sunrise, giving them a silvery glow. But despite this glow, it can be hard to differentiate NLCs from lower-altitude look-alikes. That confusion has meant extra work for project leaders.

Volunteer Namai Chandra shared, "I noticed that NLC images were being manually verified by the project leaders. It felt like a task well-suited for a human-in-the-loop machine learning pipeline, one that could handle the repetitive screening automatically, while keeping human judgment central for the images that matter most.” In other words, Namai found a way to help observers verify when they are indeed seeing NLCs and when they’re not.

Namai reached out to the Space Cloud Watch scientists Drs. Chihoko Cullens and Brentha Thurairajah, who were delighted with his idea. Namai soon developed a machine learning pipeline, training it on a variety of cloud images, including both the NLCs and the lower altitude look-alikes that are often submitted to Space Cloud Watch. The pipeline combines image pre-screening, cloud classification, and confidence-based review routing. After several rounds of development, testing, and refinement, he released his NLC identification tool to the project. This tool is now being used by cloud contributors who are unsure whether they have observed NLCs, as well as project scientists that want to flag images for review.

Grab a camera and join the Space Cloud Watch project today! If you’ve hesitated to contribute to Space Cloud Watch because you were not certain if what you were seeing was a noctilucent cloud, you now have a way to check before you share – thanks to Namai.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a volunteer-developed machine learning tool that enhances the efficiency of a NASA-supported citizen science project monitoring noctilucent clouds, which are indicators of changing atmospheric conditions. This contributes to climate science by improving data collection and analysis on a phenomenon linked to Earth's long-term weather patterns, benefiting broad environmental research efforts.
articles.personality_title: Volunteer creates tool to spot rare night-shining clouds
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Some special clouds called noctilucent clouds (NLCs) have been appearing more often and closer to the ground than before. Scientists want to understand why these changes are happening, as they might be linked to shifts in Earth's weather over many years. To help with this, NASA supports a project called Space Cloud Watch, where people worldwide take pictures of these clouds and send them to researchers.

**What happened** – A volunteer named Namai Chandra noticed that project leaders were spending a lot of time checking if cloud photos really showed NLCs or similar-looking clouds closer to the ground. He created a machine learning tool that helps volunteers and scientists quickly sort and identify true NLC images. Namai worked with the Space Cloud Watch scientists to train the tool using many cloud pictures. Now, this tool helps everyone involved by automatically screening images and highlighting those that need careful review.

**Impact** – This tool makes the work of spotting noctilucent clouds faster and more accurate. Before, people had to check every photo by hand, which took a lot of time. With this new help, the project can collect better data about these unusual clouds. This is important because understanding NLCs can tell us about changes in the atmosphere and long-term weather patterns on Earth.

**What's next step** – Volunteers who take pictures of clouds can now use this tool to check if they have caught an NLC before sending their images. This will encourage more people to join Space Cloud Watch and help scientists gather more reliable information. The project can grow and improve as more data comes in with the help of this new technology.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A volunteer’s machine learning tool is helping a NASA project quickly and accurately identify rare noctilucent clouds, improving climate research through better data collection.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un bénévole crée un outil pour repérer les rares nuages noctiluques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Certains nuages spéciaux appelés nuages noctiluques (NLC) apparaissent plus souvent et plus bas dans le ciel qu'avant. **Impact** – Cet outil rend la détection des nuages noctiluques plus rapide et plus précise. Avant, chaque photo devait être vérifiée à la main, ce qui prenait beaucoup de temps. **Résumé en une phrase** – Un outil d’apprentissage automatique développé par un bénévole aide un projet de la NASA à identifier rapidement et précisément des nuages noctiluques rares, améliorant la recherche climatique grâce à une meilleure collecte de données.
articles.personality_title_es: Un voluntario crea una herramienta para detectar raras nubes noctilucentes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Algunas nubes especiales llamadas nubes noctilucentes (NLC) están apareciendo con más frecuencia y más bajas en el cielo que antes. Los científicos quieren entender por qué suceden estos cambios, ya que podrían estar relacionados con cambios en el clima de la Tierra a largo plazo. Para ayudar, la NASA apoya un proyecto llamado Space Cloud Watch, donde personas de todo el mundo toman fotos de estas nubes y las envían a los investigadores.

**Qué pasó** – Un voluntario llamado Namai Chandra notó que los líderes del proyecto dedicaban mucho tiempo a revisar si las fotos mostraban realmente NLC o nubes parecidas a menor altura. Él creó una herramienta de aprendizaje automático que ayuda a voluntarios y científicos a ordenar e identificar rápidamente las imágenes verdaderas de NLC. Namai trabajó con los científicos de Space Cloud Watch para entrenar la herramienta con muchas fotos de nubes. Ahora, esta herramienta ayuda a todos al filtrar automáticamente las imágenes y resaltar las que necesitan revisión cuidadosa.

**Impacto** – Esta herramienta hace que detectar nubes noctilucentes sea más rápido y preciso. Antes, las personas debían revisar cada foto manualmente, lo que tomaba mucho tiempo. Con esta ayuda, el proyecto puede recopilar mejores datos sobre estas nubes especiales. Entender las NLC es importante porque muestra cambios en la atmósfera y patrones climáticos a largo plazo.

**Próximo paso** – Los voluntarios que toman fotos de nubes ahora pueden usar esta herramienta para verificar si capturaron una NLC antes de enviar sus imágenes. Esto animará a más personas a unirse a Space Cloud Watch y ayudará a los científicos a obtener información más confiable. El proyecto podrá crecer y mejorar con más datos gracias a esta nueva tecnología.

**Resumen en una frase** – Una herramienta de aprendizaje automático creada por un voluntario ayuda a un proyecto de la NASA a identificar rápida y correctamente las raras nubes noctilucentes, mejorando la investigación climática con una mejor recolección de datos.

articles.title: In Nepal, residents learn how to live alongside wild animals
articles.summary: Over the past five decades, Nepal has established itself as a model for wildlife conservation. Nearly 20 percent of the country’s territory has been designated as protected areas. Over the past five decades, Nepal has established itself as a model for wildlife conservation. Nearly 20 percent of the country’s territory has been designated as protected areas. An effective anti-poaching policy has helped save iconic species such as the one-horned rhinoceros and the gharial crocodile, which were once on the brink of extinction. But this success also comes with tragic consequences.

In the heart of Nepal's Terai plains, presented around the world as a conservation success story, animal attacks have claimed hundreds of lives. In some areas, tigers kill up to three people a month.

Tensions are rising in these communities. Residents no longer just want coexistence; they seek protection. To better understand animal movements and prevent further tragedies, civil society groups are stepping in.

FRANCE 24's Fantine Dantzer and Tashi Bista report.

articles.reasoning: The article highlights Nepal's significant achievements in wildlife conservation, including the establishment of protected areas and successful anti-poaching policies that have saved endangered species. This represents a meaningful positive impact on biodiversity and environmental protection with broad societal relevance. Although it mentions challenges related to human-wildlife conflict, the focus on conservation success and ongoing efforts to manage coexistence provides an inspiring and hopeful narrative.
articles.personality_title: Nepal balances wildlife protection with community safety
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Over the last 50 years, Nepal has worked hard to protect its wildlife. About 20% of the country is now set aside as safe places for animals. This has helped save rare animals like the one-horned rhinoceros and the gharial crocodile, which were almost extinct.

**What happened** – Nepal’s efforts have been successful, but living near wild animals can be dangerous. In the Terai plains, some tigers have attacked people, causing many deaths. Because of this, local communities want better protection alongside the animals.

**Impact** – Nepal’s story is important because it shows how protecting animals can bring big benefits but also new challenges. The country is finding ways to keep both people and wildlife safe, which is not easy but very important.

**What's next step** – Groups from civil society are working to understand where animals move and how to stop attacks. This information will help create better safety plans for people living near wild animals.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Nepal’s strong wildlife protection is saving endangered species while new efforts focus on keeping communities safe too.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le Népal équilibre protection des animaux sauvages et sécurité des habitants
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis 50 ans, le Népal travaille dur pour protéger sa faune. Environ 20 % du pays est désormais réservé comme zones sûres pour les animaux. Cela a aidé à sauver des espèces rares comme le rhinocéros à une corne et le gavial, presque disparues.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les efforts du Népal ont réussi, mais vivre près des animaux sauvages peut être dangereux. Dans les plaines du Terai, certains tigres ont attaqué des personnes, causant de nombreux décès. Les communautés locales demandent donc une meilleure protection.

**Impact** – L’histoire du Népal est importante car elle montre que protéger les animaux apporte de grands bénéfices mais aussi de nouveaux défis. Le pays cherche à protéger à la fois les humains et la faune, ce qui est difficile mais essentiel.

**Prochaine étape** – Des groupes de la société civile étudient les déplacements des animaux pour mieux prévenir les attaques. Ces informations aideront à créer des plans de sécurité pour les habitants proches des animaux sauvages.

**Phrase clé** – La forte protection de la faune au Népal sauve des espèces menacées, tout en développant des efforts pour assurer la sécurité des communautés.
articles.personality_title_es: Nepal equilibra la protección de la vida silvestre con la seguridad de las comunidades
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En los últimos 50 años, Nepal ha trabajado mucho para proteger su vida silvestre. Cerca del 20 % del país está reservado como áreas seguras para los animales. Esto ha ayudado a salvar especies raras como el rinoceronte de un solo cuerno y el gavial, que casi desaparecieron.

**Qué pasó** – Los esfuerzos de Nepal han tenido éxito, pero vivir cerca de animales salvajes puede ser peligroso. En las llanuras de Terai, algunos tigres han atacado a personas, causando muchas muertes. Por eso, las comunidades locales piden más protección.

**Impacto** – La historia de Nepal es importante porque muestra cómo proteger a los animales trae grandes beneficios, pero también nuevos retos. El país está buscando formas de mantener seguros tanto a los humanos como a la fauna, algo difícil pero esencial.

**Próximo paso** – Grupos de la sociedad civil están estudiando los movimientos de los animales para evitar ataques. Esta información ayudará a crear mejores planes de seguridad para las personas que viven cerca de animales salvajes.

**Frase clave** – La fuerte protección de la vida silvestre en Nepal está salvando especies en peligro mientras se trabaja para proteger también a las comunidades.
